sentences.text: Saurolophus represents a genus of massive ornithopod dinosaurs from the late Cretaceous period.
The North American species, S. osborni, measured approximately 8.2 meters in length with a skull spanning one meter.
Its Asian counterpart, S. angustirostris, is known from at least fifteen specimens and reached lengths of about 13 meters.
Scientists estimated the weight of S. osborni to be around three tonnes.
The larger Asian species could have weighed up to eleven tonnes.
Footprints attributed to S. angustirostris suggest it might have grown as large as Shantungosaurus.
Barnum Brown established the genus in 1912 based on fossils found in Canada.
The initial remains were discovered in early Maastrichtian rocks of the Horseshoe Canyon Formation near Tolman Ferry on the Red Deer River in Alberta.
This herbivore was capable of moving on two legs or four legs.
It used a broad beak to crop plants and a cheek-like organ to hold food in its jaws.
Saurolophus could feed on plants ranging from the ground up to about four meters high.
The skull allowed a grinding motion analogous to chewing, with teeth packed in batteries containing hundreds of teeth, only a few of which were used at once.

Studies of juveniles indicate that the adult crest was poorly developed in infancy, while the snout grew longer, the orbit became more oval, frontal doming decreased, and the coronoid process grew higher during development.
Evidence from the Dragon's Tomb bonebed provides direct proof of social behavior in S. angustirostris, but no such evidence exists for S. osborni.

The lack of large wounds on the rest of the skeleton suggests that the Tarbosaurus scavenged an already dead Saurolophus angustirostris, despite the humerus bearing three distinctive feeding marks interpreted as punctures, drag marks, and bite-and-drag marks.
Two species are currently considered valid: S. osborni and S. angustirostris.
Barnum Brown originally classified Saurolophus in its own subfamily, Saurolophinae, within Trachodontidae.

Saurolophus is a genus of two known hadrosaurid ornithopod dinosaur species that lived during the late Cretaceous, approximately 70 to 68 million years ago in the Maastrichtian, in what is now North America and Asia.

A 2001 study suggested Saurolophus osborni belonged to a distinct inland fauna associated with Anchiceratops ornatus, distinct from the coastal fauna associated with Pachyrhinosaurus canadensis and Edmontosaurus regalis.
The Nemegt Formation environment was semi-arid during certain times of the year.
The function of the distinctive spike-like crest of Saurolophus is debated, with multiple interpretations suggesting various roles.
Until a 2011 re-evaluation by Phil R. Bell, S. angustirostris was not well described.
